titulo.texto: A Miner’s Dream: The Borda Gardens

frase_gancho.texto: A man who made a fortune from the silver of Taxco built terraces, fountains and a French-style lake here.

puente_narrativo.texto: If your route continues, walk through the garden to the story of the emperors.

guion_corto.texto: José de la Borda arrived in New Spain in seventeen sixteen and made an enormous fortune from the silver mines of Taxco and Zacatecas. He probably bought this land in seventeen sixty-three, across from the old Franciscan monastery that is now the cathedral. He died here in seventeen seventy-eight. His son Manuel, who was a priest and also loved botany, turned the house into a garden of flowers and fruit trees, finished in seventeen eighty-three. It has terraces, ramps, fountains, two pools and an artificial lake, in the French style. Near the house a church dedicated to the Virgin of Guadalupe was built. Today it is a cultural center, and its history includes a difficult side: Borda’s wealth was based on the exploitation of indigenous labor.

guion_largo.texto:
This garden tells the layer of rest: the place where the rich and powerful came to retreat. But this story begins with a fortune. José de la Borda was born around sixteen ninety-nine or seventeen hundred, and the sources doubt whether it was in Spain or in France. He arrived in New Spain in seventeen sixteen, when he was about seventeen years old. He got rich with the mines of Taxco and Zacatecas. At some point he was considered the richest man in Mexico, and it is estimated that he earned about forty million pesos. With that money he paid for famous works, such as the church of Santa Prisca in Taxco and the Casa Borda in Mexico City.

He also had a life with shadows. He is criticized for having grown rich through the cruel exploitation of indigenous labor. In his last years he suffered mercury poisoning, a risk of silver mining, and retired to Cuernavaca, where his son Manuel, who was a priest, lived.

According to one source, Borda bought this land in seventeen sixty-three, across from the Franciscan convent that is now the cathedral. He died here in seventeen seventy-eight. Manuel inherited the property. He was very interested in plants, and turned the land into a garden of flowers and fruit trees. The work on the garden and the lake was finished in seventeen eighty-three.

The design follows the style of French gardens: terraces at different levels, ramps, stairs and fountains. There are two pools and a water system that fed the lake and several fountains. A Baroque fountain called the Fuente Magna is also mentioned, as is a portico with grilles that recalls the gardens of the Alhambra, in Granada. Near the house a church dedicated to the Virgin of Guadalupe was built.

The botanical collection began in the eighteenth century. It brings together plants native to Mesoamerica and exotic plants. Among the native ones, copal, flor de mayo and avocado are mentioned. Among the exotic ones are mango and jacaranda. The garden is also home to fish, birds and squirrels.

Today this place is a cultural center with exhibition rooms, a bookstore and an open-air auditorium. It is classified as a historic monument. It is best to stroll without hurry: everything in the garden is designed for looking, resting and listening to the water.

To walk through the garden, follow the water. The terraces descend in levels, and each level has its own view. Look for the stairs and ramps that join one level to another. In a French-style garden order matters: straight paths, aligned fountains and plants placed with intention.

Another way of looking is by species. The collection brings together native and exotic plants. If you see a flor de mayo, an avocado or a jacaranda, you are already reading the crossing of two botanical worlds: what grew here and what arrived from afar.

When you sit near the lake, think about the two faces of this place. It is a beautiful garden, but it was paid for with mines and other people’s labor. Beauty and difficult history walk together.

texto: Find the terraces and ramps and notice how the garden rises and falls in levels
Find the lake and the fountains and listen to the water
Look for the church of the Virgin of Guadalupe next to the house and ask who it was built for

texto.Founder: José de la Borda, silver miner of Taxco and Zacatecas
texto.Garden work: finished by his son Manuel in 1783
texto.Style: French, with terraces, ramps, fountains, two pools and an artificial lake

texto.pregunta: Myth: Emperor Maximilian built the Borda Garden.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The Borda family made it in the eighteenth century. Maximilian chose it as a summer home in eighteen sixty-five.
